articles.title: Keyboard shortcuts
articles.summary: Every key the app listens to, grouped by job. The same list opens inside the app.
articles.what: Keys listed in the in-app shortcut panel (press ?): Canvas tools: B, E, P, K, M, W, L, V, C, Shift+J, Q, R, J | Editing: Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y / Ctrl+Shift+Z, Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V, Ctrl+Shift+V, Ctrl+J, Ctrl+Shift+J, Ctrl+E, Ctrl+Shift+E, Ctrl+Shift+N, Ctrl+L, Delete, Shift+Delete, Alt+Bksp, Ctrl+Bksp, Ctrl+D, Ctrl+A, Ctrl+Shift+I | View & navigation: Ctrl+=, Ctrl+-, Ctrl+0, Space+Drag, [ / ], Ctrl+[ / ], Ctrl+Shift+[ / ], 1-9, X, ↺, Shift+V, ? | Zone operations: Ctrl+R, Shift+R, Shift+N, Shift+D, Shift+E, Shift+H, Shift+T, ? / Esc. More keys that work in the canvas: O rectangle select, Y pick item, A select all of one colour, Ctrl+T transform, Ctrl+S save a snapshot, Ctrl+G generate script, F5 refresh the preview. Zones: Alt+1 to Alt+9 pick a zone, Up and Down move through zones, Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down change priority, with the Move Selection Border tool armed, Arrow nudges the zone's drawn border 1 pixel and Shift+Arrow 10 pixels. Brush: { and } change hardness by 10. With no paint tool active, 0, 1 and 2 give fit, 100 percent and 200 percent zoom. The mouse wheel always zooms.
when: You forgot which key a tool uses.
how: Press ? to open the shortcut panel in the app.
Press ? or Esc to close it.

controls.label: M
controls.effect: Select with the elliptical marquee (the rectangle select is on O).
Make the brush smaller or larger (5 at a time); { and } change hardness.
Set the brush or layer opacity to 10 to 90 percent (0 sets 100 percent).

controls.label: X
controls.effect: Swap the foreground and background colours.
Reset the foreground and background colours.

controls.label: Shift+E
controls.effect: Show or hide the zone popout panel.

tips: Letter keys do nothing while you are typing in a text box.
Shift+E shows or hides the zone panel. E alone is the Eraser.
pitfalls: The panel says Marquee for M. M is the elliptical marquee; use O for a rectangle.
Ctrl+S saves an autosave snapshot, not a project file. Use Save project for that.

deep.heading: Number keys do three different jobs
deep.body: The keys 1 to 9 set 10 to 90 percent and 0 sets 100 percent, but where that goes depends on what is active. With a paint tool armed (Brush, Eraser, Clone, Healing, Recolor, Smudge, Burn and the like) it sets that tool's own opacity or strength. With a non-paint tool and a layer selected it sets the layer's opacity and shows a Layer opacity message. With neither, 0, 1 and 2 become zoom: fit, 100 percent and 200 percent.

deep.heading: Size and hardness keys
deep.body: [ makes the brush 5 smaller and ] makes it 5 larger. The Brush Size slider runs 1 to 300 and starts at 20, so the keys clamp at both ends. { and } change Hardness by 10 on a 0 to 100 slider that starts at 100. Hardness keys only act on tools that use hardness, and only on the Eraser when its mode is Brush. The Eraser's Block mode ignores 1 to 9 and shows a message that it is always 100 percent opaque.

deep.heading: Keys that are not obvious from the panel
deep.body: M is the elliptical marquee although the panel calls it Marquee; O is the rectangle. A selects all pixels of one colour, Y picks an item, and Shift+J is the Healing brush while plain J is Burn. F5 refreshes the live preview and aborts a stuck one. Ctrl+Shift+R reloads the last paint and is not in the panel. With the Move Selection Border tool armed, the arrow keys nudge the current zone's drawn border 1 pixel, or 10 with Shift. Alt+arrow also nudges there (1 pixel, 5 with Shift) but only in that tool; with any other tool armed it moves nothing.

deep.heading: Zone keys versus tool keys
deep.body: Bare letters are tools, while Shift+letter keys are zone actions: Shift+N new zone, Shift+D duplicate, Shift+R randomise, Shift+E show or hide the zone panel. That is why E alone is the Eraser. Alt+1 to Alt+9 pick a zone, Up and Down walk through zones, and Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down change its priority.

examples.title: Paint a soft edge fast
examples.goal: Get a soft 60-pixel brush at half strength without touching a slider.

settings.Brush Size: 20 then press ] ten times for 70, or [ twice for 10
settings.Hardness: press { five times to go from 100 to 50

examples.result: The Brush is armed, the size and Hardness sliders move as you press, and the brush opacity reads 50 percent.

examples.title: Compare before and after on a layer
examples.goal: Dim a selected layer and then check the whole paint.
examples.result: Move is not a paint tool, so 4 sets the layer to 40 percent with a Layer opacity message. 0 puts it back to 100 percent.

examples.title: Zone round trip with no mouse
examples.goal: Add a zone, shuffle its finish and render.
examples.result: A new zone appears and is selected, Shift+R gives it a random look, Alt+1 jumps back to Zone 1, and Ctrl+R starts a render.

combos.why: A shorter version to learn first: tool keys, then Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+D and Ctrl+R.
Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y are in the table; the Undo History menu steps back many actions at once.
Ctrl+0, Ctrl+= and Ctrl+- and the 0, 1, 2 keys all change zoom.
Shift+N, Shift+D and Shift+R do what the zone card buttons do.

faq.q: Why does pressing a letter do nothing?
faq.a: Keys are ignored while the cursor is in a text box, number box or dropdown. Click on the canvas or empty space, then press the key.

faq.q: Does Ctrl+S save my project?
faq.a: No. It only refreshes a local autosave snapshot and shows Autosave snapshot saved locally. To keep a project file use the Save SHOKK button.

faq.q: Why did 5 zoom or change opacity instead of what I expected?
faq.a: Number keys change meaning with the active tool. A paint tool gets opacity, a selected layer with a non-paint tool gets layer opacity, and with neither the keys 0, 1 and 2 zoom.

faq.q: What is the key for a rectangle selection?
faq.a: O. The panel labels M as Marquee, but M is the elliptical marquee.

faq.q: Is there a key I will not find in the panel?
faq.a: Yes. Ctrl+Shift+R reloads the last paint, Ctrl+G generates a script, F5 refreshes the preview, and the arrow keys nudge a zone's border while the Move Selection Border tool is armed.

faq.q: Does the Eraser respond to the opacity keys?
faq.a: Soft does. Block Eraser is always 100 percent opaque and the keys show a message instead.

mistakes.symptom: Pressing E hides or shows the zone panel, or you expected it to.
mistakes.cause: E alone is the Eraser. The zone panel toggle is Shift+E.
mistakes.fix: Use Shift+E for the zone panel and E for erasing.

mistakes.cause: The armed tool has no size or no hardness, such as a selection tool, or the Eraser is in Block or clear-all mode.
mistakes.fix: Arm the Brush or another size tool first. For the Eraser, switch its mode to Brush.

mistakes.symptom: You pressed Ctrl+S and expected a saved file.
mistakes.cause: Ctrl+S saves only a local autosave snapshot.
mistakes.fix: Click Save SHOKK to write a project file you can reopen.

protips: With the Move Selection Border tool armed, Arrow nudges the zone's drawn border by 1 pixel and Shift+Arrow by 10. It is the quickest way to line up an edge without redrawing.
F5 is the rescue key when the live preview looks stuck: it aborts the stuck refresh and starts a new one.

articles.title: Control index: where is every control
articles.summary: Every slider, button, switch and box has its own page. This index shows which area of the app each one lives in.
articles.what: Each control page tells you what it does, its range and starting value, and where to find it. Search for the control by its label, or start from the area. Window, top bar, dialogs: 139 controls, start with "The window tour: header, toolbar, zones, centre, right column, render". Tools, tool options, selection: 167 controls, start with "Keyboard shortcuts: the ones worth learning". Zones: 41 controls, start with "Zone card controls: mute, lock, reset, duplicate, delete". layer list: 71 controls, start with "The layer list". Finish picker and library: 35 controls, start with "The finish picker, library and browser". Base colour and base settings: 17 controls, start with "Base strength, hue, saturation and brightness". Patterns: 11 controls, start with "What a pattern is". Spec controls: 14 controls, start with "R, G and B channel sliders". Preview and render: 30 controls, start with "The Render button and render size (2048 / 1024)". Undo History: 3 controls, start with "Undo History panel". Spec Sculpt Lab: 232 controls, start with "Spec Sculpt: the rest of the controls". Shokk Drop: 60 controls, start with "shokk_drop.overview". Settings: 10 controls, start with "The Settings gear: what is in it". AI copilot panel: 8 controls, start with "ai_copilot.overview".
when: You see a control and want to know what it does.
You know the job but not where the control is.
how: Search for the label you see on screen.
Open the control page for the range, starting value and place.
Or open the area article first and follow its list.
tips: A page says where the control is, for example Pro > right column > layer list.
Controls that the app builds on the fly (such as layer rows) are covered by their area article.

deep.heading: How big the index is
deep.body: The app has 838 documented controls, each with its own page: 139 in the window, top bar and dialogs, 167 in tools and tool options, 41 in zones, 71 in layers, 35 in the finish picker, 17 in base colour, 11 in patterns, 14 in spec, 30 in preview and render, 3 in undo history, 232 in Spec Sculpt Lab, 60 in Shokk Drop, 10 in settings and 8 in the AI copilot panel. Spec Sculpt Lab alone is more than a quarter of the list.

deep.heading: What a control page tells you
deep.body: Every page states where the control lives, for example in the zone popout panel, the tool options bar or the right column. Sliders also give their range and starting value. Of the 838 pages, 138 list a range and 181 list a starting value, because buttons and switches have neither. Brush Size shows 1 to 300 starting at 20, Hue Shift shows -180 to 180 starting at 0, and Base Strength shows 0 to 100 percent starting at 100 percent.

deep.heading: Same label, different place
deep.body: Some labels exist in more than one spot, and each place has its own page. R Metal appears in the spec strip under the preview, in the preview's spec pane, in the full-size preview window and in the zone popout panel's Spec section. Only the zone panel version has the -127 to 127 range in steps of 5. Spec strength in Spec Sculpt Lab runs 0 to 200 while the zone Spec Strength runs 0 to 100 in steps of 5. Always check the where line before trusting a number.

deep.heading: What is not in the index
deep.body: Controls that the app builds while you work, such as one row per layer, are covered by the area article instead of by individual pages. Search by the label you see and, if nothing matches, look for the area article.

examples.title: Find the right Hue Shift
examples.goal: Look up the range of a slider you can see on screen.

settings.Where it says it lives: zone popout panel (click a zone card)

examples.result: You learn that 0 leaves colours alone and the extremes turn them half way around the colour wheel.

examples.goal: Decide which Spec Strength you are looking at.

combos.why: Keys are controls too: use the table when the control has a shortcut.
The zone card buttons are the 41 zone controls.
The biggest area, 232 controls, is covered by this article.
If you do not know which area a control is in, tour the window first.

faq.q: How do I find a control I can see but cannot name?
faq.a: Search for the exact words printed on it. Each control page is named after its on-screen label, so the label is the best search word.

faq.q: Why does one control have several pages?
faq.a: The same label can exist in more than one place, such as R Metal in the spec strip, the preview's spec pane and the zone popout panel. Each place has its own page and range.

faq.q: Do all controls list a range and a starting value?
faq.a: No. Only sliders and number boxes do. Buttons, switches and menus show where they are and what they do.

faq.q: Where is a layer row control documented?
faq.a: Layer rows are built while you work, so the Layers area article covers them instead of one page per row.

faq.q: Is the control list the same for every build?
faq.a: The pages are generated from the controls in this version of the app, so they follow the version you have.

mistakes.symptom: A number you read for a slider does not match the slider on your screen.
mistakes.cause: The same label lives in more than one place with different ranges, for example Spec Strength 0 to 100 in a zone and 0 to 200 in Spec Sculpt Lab.
mistakes.fix: Open the page whose where line matches the panel you are in.

mistakes.symptom: You searched for a layer row button and found nothing.
mistakes.cause: Rows the app builds on the fly have no pages of their own.
mistakes.fix: Look at the layer list (right column) article and read its list.

protips: The where line starts with the mode and column, so reading it tells you which tab or panel to open before you start hunting through the screen.
Slider ranges show what the number means. Base Strength steps in 5s from 0 to 100, so you can hit 100 exactly, while Hue Shift steps in 1s.
articles.screens_exempt: Alphabetical index that points at controls described (and pictured) in their own articles; the index itself has no screen.

articles.title: Glossary
articles.summary: Plain-words meaning of the terms the app uses, from spec map and tolerance to PSD and zone order.
articles.what: User ID: Your User ID is your iRacing Customer ID, 4 to 7 digits. | Custom Number vs Sim-Stamped: Custom Number saves your paint as car_num_<ID>; Sim-Stamped saves it as car_<ID> and iRacing stamps your number on. | iRacing: iRacing is the sim your paint goes into. | Reload in iRacing (Ctrl+R): After a render, press Ctrl+R in iRacing to reload the car textures; the car flashes white and shows the new paint. | iRacing Car Folder: The Car Folder is the iRacing paint folder for ONE car (a folder, not a file). | Where my files go: Every render copies the paint and the spec file into your iRacing Car Folder. | It does not show in iRacing: When the paint does not show in iRacing it is almost always the User ID, the number setting, the car folder or a missing Ctrl+R. | Spec map: The spec file tells iRacing how shiny each part is: red is metal, green is roughness, blue is clearcoat. | Metallic (red channel): In the spec file the red channel is how metal a part is: 255 is solid metal, 0 is paint or plastic. | Roughness (green channel): In the spec file the green channel is roughness: 0 is a perfect mirror, 255 is rough and dull. | Clearcoat (blue channel): In the spec file the blue channel is the clearcoat: 16 is the shiniest, 255 is dull and 0-15 means none. | The .mip file: iRacing builds a .mip file from your spec the first time it loads it. | Trading Paints: Trading Paints is how other drivers get your files, because iRacing never shares textures between drivers. | Paint size (2048): iRacing paints must be exactly 2048 x 2048 (or 1024 x 1024). | TGA files: iRacing wants a 24-bit TGA. | Template layers: Wire and Mask are guides, not paint. Car_Mandatory is real template art for the headlight and grill mesh. | Zone limit: A render accepts up to 50 zones, but only about 20 zones that have their own painted area fit in memory. | Render time / slow render: A render usually takes seconds to about a minute; more zones and heavy finishes take longer. | Preview vs the real thing: The live preview is a quick design view. | Auto-deploy: The car folder is what puts files into iRacing. | ZIP package: Turn on Export ZIP Package in Settings and each render also builds a ZIP to download. | Helmets and suits: Shokker paints cars in this build, not helmets or suits. | Wheels: Wheels, rims and tyres are not on the car paint sheet: iRacing paints them from a separate wheel texture. | Windows and glass: The windows are not part of the paint on most iRacing cars; the sim draws the glass. | Cockpit and interior: The cockpit, roll bar and pit box are only paintable if your template has a layer for them. | Small car parts: Small parts like lights, grilles and mirrors are usually drawn inside a bigger panel on the paint sheet, not as their own area. | Project file (.spb / .shokk): The Shokker project file holds your whole design so you can reopen and keep editing. | Recipe (sharing a design): A recipe is a block of text (or a .shokkerrecipe file) that rebuilds a design on any car Shokker knows. | Settings: Most settings are in the top bar; the rest (Auto-deploy, ZIP export, Report a Problem, License) are under the Settings gear at the top right. | Report a problem: Report a Problem builds a copy-paste bundle of recent errors and logs. | AI copilot and key: The built-in helper works fully offline and free. | Hue / saturation / brightness: Hue, saturation and brightness are three sliders that shift a finish's colour. | Tolerance: Tolerance is how fuzzy a colour match is: low grabs that exact shade, high grabs the whole neighbourhood. | Hard edge: Hard Edge makes a zone's boundary crisp instead of a soft blend. | Strength / opacity: Strength and opacity control how strongly a finish or pattern shows. | Pattern size / scale: Scale makes a pattern bigger or smaller; on a whole car, fine detail looks richest, so crush the scale down. | Zone order (which wins): When zones overlap, the zone higher in the list wins. | Lock: The lock on the BASE row stops Randomize from changing the base. LOCK ZONE on a layer card is a different lock: it ties a zone to one layer. | Beta / known issues: Shokker is in beta: some finishes are being rebuilt. | What can the helper do: Ask in plain words: change a colour, add a look, fix why something does not show, or ask how any button works. | Spec Sculpt Lab: Spec Sculpt is a full-page workshop that builds a spec map from a paint image on its own, outside the zone flow. | Shokk Drop: Shokk Drop imports your own artwork or a DNA spec and shares finishes as .spbdrop packs. | Finish Viewer: The Finish Viewer lets you window-shop the whole library as thumbnails. | PSD vs TGA: A layered PSD gives each layer its own zone, so finishes never bleed onto sponsors or numbers. | Car number vs User ID: Your User ID (Customer ID) is not your car number. | Make it look expensive: To make a car pop: pair a colour with its opposite on the wheel, keep one hero panel, and let a fine-detail spec do the sparkle. | Foundation finishes: Foundation finishes change only the shine and keep your paint colours exactly as they are. | Make it pop: To make a car pop, add contrast: pair a colour with its opposite and let the shine do the sparkle. | Layer effects (shadow, glow, bevel): Layer effects add a drop shadow, outer glow, stroke, colour overlay or bevel to a layer, like in an image editor. | Selection & masks: A selection or mask limits where a change lands. | Blur, sharpen & adjustments: Image tools like blur, sharpen and brightness work on the pixels of a layer; for finishes use zones instead. | Keyboard shortcuts: Keyboard shortcuts are listed under the Settings gear.
when: A word in the app or in a help answer is new to you.
how: Find the term in the list.
Read the short meaning next to it.
Open the linked article for the full story.
tips: Ask the AI copilot "what is <term>" for the same answer in chat.

deep.heading: The four groups of words
deep.body: The list above falls into four groups. Getting the paint into iRacing: User ID, Car Folder, Custom Number vs Sim-Stamped, Ctrl+R, Auto-deploy, ZIP package, Trading Paints. How shine works: Spec map, Metallic, Roughness, Clearcoat, the .mip file, Foundation finishes. How you build a look: zone, Tolerance, Hard edge, Strength, Scale, Zone order, Lock, Hue, saturation and brightness. What the car sheet can and cannot paint: paint size, TGA, wheels, windows, cockpit and small parts.

deep.heading: Spec numbers in one line each
deep.body: Red is metal: 0 is paint or plastic and 255 is solid metal. Green is roughness: 0 is a perfect mirror and 255 is rough and dull. Blue is clearcoat: 16 is the shiniest, 255 is dull and 0 to 15 means no clearcoat. iRacing builds a .mip file from your spec the first time it loads it. The full table is in the Spec value cheat sheet article.

deep.heading: Words that sound alike but are not the same
deep.body: User ID is your iRacing Customer ID (4 to 7 digits) and is not your car number. A Car Folder is the paint folder for one car and is a folder, not a file. Strength is how strongly a finish shows; Tolerance is how wide a colour match is; Scale is how big a pattern is. The lock on the BASE row stops Randomize, while LOCK ZONE on a layer card ties a zone to a single layer.

deep.heading: Limits worth knowing
deep.body: A render accepts up to 50 zones, but only about 20 zones that have their own painted area fit in memory. Paints must be exactly 2048 by 2048 (or 1024 by 1024) and a 24-bit TGA. A render usually takes seconds to about a minute, and more zones or heavy finishes take longer. Shokker paints cars in this build, not helmets or suits.

examples.title: My paint does not show in iRacing
examples.goal: Find out why a rendered paint is missing in the sim.

settings.Check 1: User ID is your Customer ID
settings.Check 2: Number setting: Custom Number vs Sim-Stamped
settings.Check 3: Car Folder is the folder for that one car

examples.result: Almost every missing-paint problem is one of these four. After Ctrl+R the car flashes white and then shows the new paint.

examples.title: Choose between Hard edge and Tolerance
examples.goal: Make a zone's boundary crisp without grabbing more colours.
examples.result: Hard Edge only changes how the boundary blends. Tolerance decides which shades are picked in the first place.

combos.why: The cheat sheet gives the full spec number table behind the spec words.
Tolerance has its own article with the full range.

faq.q: Is my User ID the same as my car number?
faq.a: No. The User ID is your iRacing Customer ID, 4 to 7 digits. The car number is separate.

faq.q: Why does my spec not do anything in Trading Paints?
faq.a: Trading Paints takes the spec only as a .mip file, so a TGA is not the spec for Trading Paints.

faq.q: What does Foundation mean?
faq.a: Foundation finishes change only the shine and keep your paint colours as they are.

faq.q: Can Shokker paint helmets, wheels or windows?
faq.a: Not helmets or suits in this build. Wheels come from a separate iRacing wheel texture and windows are drawn by the sim.

mistakes.symptom: The paint is in the folder but does not show in the sim.
mistakes.cause: The wrong User ID, the wrong number setting, the wrong Car Folder or no Ctrl+R.
mistakes.fix: Check those four in order and press Ctrl+R in iRacing after the render.

mistakes.cause: Zone order: a higher zone in the list wins where zones overlap.
mistakes.fix: Drag the zone higher in the list, or narrow the zone above it.

protips: Ask the AI copilot what is followed by the word to get the same answer in the chat.
When a word has two meanings, such as lock, open its linked article before you act.
articles.screens_exempt: Pure reference list of words and what they mean; it describes no single screen or action, so a picture would be decoration.

when: You type a colour into the AI copilot box and want to know which words work.
You want an exact shade by name.
how: Type the colour name in your request, for example "make the hood burgundy".
If the shade is not right, add a word such as light, dark or deep.
Or pick the exact colour with the colour picker.
tips: Two-word names such as antique gold work.
For an exact match, use the colour picker or a hex code.
pitfalls: Some words name a finish, not a colour. Chrome, candy and pearl are finishes.
An extra name outside the core list will not set a zone colour. Use a core name, the colour picker or a hex code.

deep.heading: Two lists, two jobs
deep.body: The designer in the AI copilot panel sets zone colours from a core list of 102 names, each tied to one exact colour: burgundy is #6d0f1f, gold #d7a72b, grabber blue #1f6fc5. The finish advisor also reads about 370 extra names such as antique gold, aquamarine or british racing green, so it can recommend finishes for them. A name outside the core list may not paint a zone when you type it; use the nearest core name or a six-digit hex code.

deep.heading: How a typed word becomes a colour
deep.body: Your sentence is lowercased and stripped of punctuation. Longer names are tried first, so dark green is read as one colour and not as dark plus green. Colours are used in the order you wrote them, each name once. A name that follows no, not, without, except or instead of is skipped, so red white and blue with no red gives white and blue. A six-digit hex code such as #1f6fc5 is taken as written and counts as an exact colour.

deep.heading: Shade words: dark, deep, light, pale, bright, neon
deep.body: If you type one of these directly before a colour that has no entry of its own, the colour is adjusted in lightness. Dark or deep caps the lightness at 30 percent. Light or pale raises it to at least 72 percent and cuts saturation by a fifth. Bright or neon sets lightness to 50 percent and raises saturation. Names that already exist, such as dark red, light blue or neon green, use their own listed colour instead.

deep.heading: Changing a colour that is already there
deep.body: When the part already has a coloured paint and you ask for another colour without giving a hex, the app turns the hue and keeps the shading, as in shifted to purple, keeping the shading. That only happens when both colours are clearly coloured; for white, black or grey it paints a flat colour. Words like darker, lighter, brighter and faded adjust the existing colour instead: darker and deeper take brightness down by 35, lighter adds 35 and trims saturation by 10, brighter adds 45 saturation, faded takes off 55.

examples.title: Name a colour
examples.goal: Paint the roof a named colour.
examples.result: The roof zone gets that exact deep red. If the roof already had a coloured, shaded paint, you may instead see a hue shift that keeps the shading.

examples.title: Make a shade with a modifier
examples.goal: Get a colour the list does not have.
examples.result: You get a deep burnt orange. Dark orange has no entry of its own, so the shade rule builds it.

examples.title: Exact match with a hex code
examples.goal: Use a team colour that has no name.
examples.result: The code is taken exactly and is treated as an exact colour. #1f6fc5 is also the listed value of grabber blue.

examples.title: Leave a colour out
examples.goal: Describe a scheme and exclude one colour.

settings.You type: white car with blue stripes, no red

examples.result: Red follows the word no, so it is skipped and only white and blue are used.

combos.why: When the word is not close enough, pick the exact colour with the colour picker.
After the colour is in, Hue Shift, Saturation and Brightness fine-tune it.
Check which Base Color option decides whether the named colour or the source paint shows.

faq.q: Does grey or gray matter?
faq.a: No. Both are the same colour, #8a8d92.

faq.q: Do spelling mistakes still work?
faq.a: Often, yes. The designer cleans common typos and text-speak first, for example blak for black, before it looks for colour names.

faq.q: Why did saying gold or silver not give me a metal finish?
faq.a: A colour name only chooses the colour. Chrome, candy, pearl and metallic are finishes, picked separately. The advisor also treats gold flake or silver chrome as a finish, not the car colour.

faq.q: Can I use a hex code in my request?
faq.a: Yes, as a six-digit code with a leading hash, such as #1f6fc5. It is used exactly as written.

faq.q: What happens when I name two colours?
faq.a: They are taken in the order you wrote them and each name is used once,. Order matters when you describe a scheme with several colours.

faq.q: How close will the result look to my word?
faq.a: Each name is one fixed colour, so burgundy is always #6d0f1f. If your idea of the shade differs, add dark, light, bright or pale, or use the colour picker.

mistakes.symptom: Your colour word painted nothing, or the wrong colour.
mistakes.cause: It may be outside the core 102 names, or a finish word such as chrome or candy.
mistakes.fix: Use a nearby core name, add a shade word, or type a hex code.

mistakes.symptom: dark pink gave a different colour than expected.
mistakes.cause: Dark pink is not a listed name, so the shade rule is applied to pink and caps lightness at 30 percent. That gives a very dark pink.
mistakes.fix: Choose a listed name such as wine or maroon, or pick the colour with the picker.

mistakes.symptom: A colour you wanted left out still appears.
mistakes.cause: The exclusion word must come right before the colour, such as no red, or before a short list joined by or. A word further away does not exclude it.
mistakes.fix: Put no, not or without right before the colour name.

protips: A hex code is treated as an exact colour: the app paints it flat instead of turning the hue of the paint already there, so use one when you want the colour to land precisely.
To make an existing colour darker without choosing a new one, say darker or deeper: it moves the existing colour's brightness down by 35 and keeps the shading.
articles.screens_exempt: Pure reference table of colour names and their hex values; there is no window or control to picture, and a screenshot would only repeat the table.

when: You want to browse by theme rather than search.
You want to know which shelf holds a look.
how: Find the shelf that matches your idea.
Open the finish picker and pick that shelf.
Click a finish and look at the preview.
tips: Most Foundation finishes change only the shine and keep your paint colours; 5 of the 25 bring their own colours.

deep.heading: What a shelf tells you and what it does not
deep.body: A shelf is a theme, not a material. Two shelves with the same family name can be opposites: in the measured averages, FRACTURED ELEMENTS sits around 57 metal with 22 of its 60 finishes having none, while FRACTURED OPALFIRE sits around 242 metal with all 50 at full metal and a low roughness of about 31. Use the shelf to find an idea and the finish card or See on paint to judge the shine.

deep.heading: Spec character by shelf (measured averages)
deep.body: Metal-heavy: FRACTURED OPALFIRE (metal about 242, roughness about 31), FRACTURED SOULS (242 and 55), FRACTURED MINDS (241 and 61), FRACTURED FORGE (233 and 60) and Color Clash (209). Flat and dull: DARK CITY (metal about 43, roughness about 161, 23 of 50 matte), ALL THAT (50 and 128), WORLD OF COLOR (38 and 106, 59 of 100 with no metal) and Sock Hop (roughness about 162). Glossy heritage: RISING SUN has 25 of 52 at high gloss. Big mixed shelves sit in the middle: More Bases about 99 metal and 93 roughness.

deep.heading: Foundation: exact shine values
deep.body: The plain Foundation materials are pure shine, listed as metal, roughness and clearcoat: Gloss 0, 30, 16; Wet Look 0, 15, 16; Satin 0, 95, 70; Matte 0, 200, 160; Flat Black 0, 250, 255; Candy 200, 15, 16; Chrome 255, 2, 16. Roughness 2 is close to a mirror and clearcoat 16 is the glossiest. Of the 25 finishes on the shelf, 5 are not plain: Orchid Shift Pearl, Moonstone, Dragon's Pearl Scale, Sentient Polycarbonate and Black Diamond Candy bring their own colours.

deep.heading: Own colours or yours
deep.body: Nearly every themed shelf brings its own colours. The ones that mostly take your zone colour are Foundation (20 of 25), Foundation EFX (41 of 46), and the specials shelves Depth and Geometry (about 76 percent), Surface and Grain (about 67 percent) and Light and Optics (about 62 percent). The total of 4,755 counts 4,137 finishes plus 317 patterns and 301 spec patterns; the finishes alone are 4,137 across 59 shelves.

faq.q: Why does the list say 4,755 but other pages say 4,137?
faq.a: 4,755 counts finishes, patterns and spec patterns together. The 4,137 finishes are the ones on the 59 shelves.

faq.q: Which shelf has the most finishes?
faq.a: More Specials, with 1,158, then More Bases with 449. They collect finishes that do not belong to a themed shelf, and most of them are not listed in the picker (ask the AI copilot for them by name).

faq.q: Which shelf should I use if I want a pure shine change?
faq.a: Foundation. Its plain materials are only metal, roughness and clearcoat, so they change the shine and let your paint colours show.

faq.q: Do Foundation finishes always keep my colours?
faq.a: Not all. 20 of the 25 take your colour. The other 5, such as Moonstone, bring their own.

faq.q: Is a Fractured shelf always glossy metal?
faq.a: No. FRACTURED ELEMENTS averages only about 57 metal, while FRACTURED OPALFIRE averages about 242.

faq.q: What are the numbers I see in the list?
faq.a: The number in brackets is how many finishes sit on the shelf, such as ASTRA 50 or SHOKK WORKS 89.

mistakes.symptom: You picked a themed finish and your paint colours disappeared.
mistakes.cause: Most shelves bring their own colours. Only Foundation, Foundation EFX and a few specials shelves mostly take yours.
mistakes.fix: Set Base Color to Use source paint, or choose a finish from Foundation or Foundation EFX.

mistakes.symptom: A shelf named after one theme gave a very different shine than another shelf of the same family.
mistakes.cause: A shelf name is a theme, not a material. Metal averages range from about 38 to 242 across shelves.
mistakes.fix: Read the finish card and use See on paint before you commit.

protips: Sort your idea by shine first: pick a metal-heavy shelf for mirror looks, a low-metal shelf for flat ones, and only then browse for the pattern or theme you like.
Candy and Chrome are both Foundation materials with 16 clearcoat; Candy is 200 metal and 15 roughness, Chrome is 255 and 2, so Chrome is the harder mirror.

articles.title: Spec value cheat sheet
articles.summary: The three spec numbers on one page: red is metal, green is roughness, blue is clearcoat.
articles.what: Red (metal): 0 is paint or plastic, 255 is full metal. Green (roughness): 0 is a mirror, 255 is rough and dull. Blue (clearcoat): 16 is the shiniest coat, 255 is dull, 0 to 15 means no clearcoat. Chrome: red 255, green near 0, blue 16, with near-white paint under it. Matte paint: red 0, green high, blue 255. Where metal is below 240, keep roughness at 15 or more. Do not use blue values 1 to 15: the app raises them to 16. In the full-car render every clearcoat is lifted to at least 16, except on Shokk Drop finishes you uploaded yourself. Decal kit values (metal, roughness, clearcoat): Flat Vinyl 0, 100, 110. Satin Decal 0, 100, 75. Gloss Decal 0, 42, 22.
when: You are setting metal, roughness or clearcoat and want the numbers at a glance.
A part looks too dull or too shiny.
how: Decide the look: mirror, satin, matte or metal.
Set red for metal, green for roughness and blue for clearcoat using the table above.

controls.label: Red (metal)
controls.effect: 255 is full metal, 0 is paint or plastic.

controls.label: Green (roughness)
controls.effect: 0 is a perfect mirror, 255 is rough and dull.

controls.label: Blue (clearcoat)
controls.effect: 16 is the shiniest, 255 is dull, 0 means no clearcoat.

tips: Low roughness plus high metal is chrome. High roughness is matte or brushed.
A chrome part needs near-white paint under it, because iRacing multiplies the paint colour by the metal.
pitfalls: A clearcoat of 255 makes even a chrome part look dull.
Without a spec file iRacing keeps the normal material: colours show but shine and chrome do not.

deep.heading: The three rules that always apply
deep.body: Clearcoat (blue) is either exactly 0 or 16 and up; the values 1 to 15 cause blown-out highlights in iRacing, so the app raises them to 16. Where metal (red) is below 240, roughness (green) is held at 15 or more, and only pixels at 240 metal or higher may go below 15 for a true mirror. The final whole-car render also lifts every clearcoat to at least 16, so a plain finish will not leave 0 in the exported map. Only uploaded Shokk Drop finishes keep their own exact clearcoat, including a deliberate 0.

deep.heading: Real values to compare against
deep.body: Metal, roughness, clearcoat for the Foundation materials: Chrome 255, 2, 16. Candy 200, 15, 16. Metallic 200, 50, 16. Satin Chrome 250, 45, 40. Pearl 100, 40, 16. Wet Look 0, 15, 16. Gloss 0, 30, 16. Satin 0, 95, 70. Matte 0, 200, 160. Flat Black 0, 250, 255. Read the first number as how metallic, the second as how rough, the third as how dull the coat is (16 is the glossiest).

deep.heading: Why a metal needs light paint
deep.body: iRacing multiplies the paint colour by the metal level in the spec. A fully metallic part painted a normal colour therefore turns dark, and a chrome part has to be painted white or close to it. A clearcoat of 255 also dulls the part: it has no coat reflection, so even chrome looks flat.

deep.heading: Reading the numbers off your own car
deep.body: Open MASK > Advanced spec utilities and choose Material Sampler to see the Spec Map, Channels and Values window. Click the map to read M, R, CC and A at that spot. Sample size can be Point, 3 by 3 Median or 5 by 5 Median; the median ignores a single stray flake. Copy M/R/CC/A copies the four numbers, and Apply to Active Zone transfers them to the zone you have selected.

combos.why: Explains what the spec map is before you read numbers off it.
Goes deeper on why 16 is the glossiest and 255 the dullest.
The full list of floors the app enforces.
The Decal Rescue Kit values above come from this tool.

faq.q: Why is blue backwards?
faq.a: Because it measures how little clearcoat there is. 16 is the strongest coat and glossiest, 255 is no coat reflection and dull.

faq.q: Can I set blue to 5 for a bit of coat?
faq.a: No. Values 1 to 15 cause blown-out highlights in iRacing and the app raises them to 16. Use 16 or higher.

faq.q: Why can chrome have roughness 2 but a satin metal cannot go below 15?
faq.a: Mirror pixels at 240 metal and above may go below 15. Below 240 metal the app keeps roughness at 15 or more.

faq.q: Why does my chrome look dark?
faq.a: The paint under it was a normal colour, which iRacing multiplies by the metal. Paint it white or near white.

faq.q: What happens if I do not make a spec file?
faq.a: iRacing keeps the car's normal material. Colours show but chrome and shine do not.

faq.q: Is 0 in blue allowed?
faq.a: It means no clearcoat in iRacing, but the usual whole-car render lifts it to 16. Only uploaded Shokk Drop finishes keep a deliberate 0.

mistakes.symptom: A chrome part looks dull and grey.
mistakes.cause: Blue is set high, for example 255, so the coat has no reflection, or the paint underneath is dark.
mistakes.fix: Use blue 16 and paint the part white or near white.

mistakes.symptom: A value you typed in blue between 1 and 15 comes out as 16.
mistakes.cause: The app raises that range to 16 on purpose because it blows out highlights in iRacing.
mistakes.fix: Pick 16 or more, and expect 16 as the glossiest.

mistakes.symptom: A rough finish with high metal looks too shiny.
mistakes.cause: Roughness was set too low. Below 240 metal the app holds it at 15 or more, but 15 is still very glossy.
mistakes.fix: Raise green to 60 or more for a satin metal, and 140 or more for matte metallic.

protips: Compare against a finish you already like: sample it with the Material Sampler and use the numbers as your target instead of guessing.
Satin Chrome is 250, 45, 40: nearly full metal but with a rougher surface and a weaker coat than Chrome.
